facts.text: Decision logic is the set of rules inside a system that converts object detection into doing nothing, warning the operator or applying the brakes.
facts.quote: Decision logic is the set of rules inside the system that turns "there is an object over there" into "do nothing", "warn the operator" or "apply the brakes".

facts.text: Decision logic takes inputs comprising sensor-derived object position and movement; machine speed, direction, steering or articulation and load; and predicted stopping distance. Decision logic outputs the stages of intervention.
facts.quote: Its inputs are the object's position and movement from the sensors; the machine's speed, direction, steering or articulation and load; and the predicted stopping distance. Its outputs are the stages of intervention.

facts.text: Road systems mostly trigger braking using phased time-to-collision thresholds or when object distance equals required stopping distance (“time to brake”), with extra conditions to suppress false alarms. Time to collision is distance divided by closing speed.
facts.quote: brake when the time to collision (distance divided by closing speed) falls below a threshold, staged by phase, or when the distance to the object equals the required stopping distance ("time to brake"), with extra conditions to suppress false alarms

facts.text: Road-system time-to-collision rules transfer poorly to job sites because near zero closing speed, time to collision becomes huge or unstable even when a person is centimeters away.
facts.quote: near zero closing speed, time to collision becomes huge or unstable even when a person is centimeters away

facts.text: Two machines with the same time to collision can need very different stopping distances on grade or mud, limiting transfer of road-system decision rules to job sites.
facts.quote: two machines with the same time to collision need very different distances on grade or mud

facts.text: Articulation and track counter-rotation can cause collisions without forward closing speed, limiting time-to-collision-based decision logic on job sites.
facts.quote: articulation and track counter-rotation can collide with no forward closing speed

facts.text: A stationary machine about to start has no time to collision, limiting time-to-collision-based decision logic on job sites.
facts.quote: a stationary machine about to start has no time to collision at all

facts.text: ISO 21815-3 sizes an off-road collision-risk area from machine kinematics and requires the collision-system distance to cover detection, confirmation and determination, action, machine stopping and a safe distance.
facts.quote: ISO 21815-3 sizes a collision-risk area from the machine's kinematics: the collision-system distance must cover detection, confirmation and determination, action, machine stopping and a safe distance

facts.text: ISO 21815-3 specifies intervention at collision-risk level 4 or above and permits a warning before intervention.
facts.quote: intervention happens at collision-risk level 4 or above, with a warning permitted before it

facts.text: The booklet's practical stopping margin is M = R - (D_perception + D_decision + D_action + D_stop + D_safe), where R is distance along the predicted path to the collision point and the subtracted sum represents everything the machine needs.
facts.quote: a margin, `M = R - (D_perception + D_decision + D_action + D_stop + D_safe)`, where R is the distance along the predicted path to the collision point and the bracket is everything the machine needs

facts.text: In the booklet's stopping-margin decision logic, positive M means margin remains, while falling or negative M raises the risk level.
facts.quote: Positive M means margin remains; a falling or negative M raises the risk level.

facts.text: The stopping-distance term D_stop should be a conservative prediction including grade, speed, load, surface, brake state and articulation.
facts.quote: D_stop should be a conservative prediction that includes grade, speed, load, surface, brake state and articulation

facts.text: The booklet's warn-or-brake flow computes stopping margin from speed, grade, load, surface and delays after an object is detected and confirmed near the predicted path. A healthy margin leads to showing the object and continued monitoring only.
facts.quote: A["Object detected and confirmed near the predicted path"] --> B["Compute the stopping margin M from speed, grade, load, surface and delays"]

facts.text: When stopping margin is unhealthy but the operator still has time, the booklet's decision flow issues an urgent warning through sound, light or seat vibration.
facts.quote: C -->|No, but the operator still has time| E["Urgent warning: sound, light or seat vibration"]

facts.text: After an urgent warning, the booklet's decision flow stands down and continues monitoring if measured operator deceleration is sufficient; otherwise, the system automatically slows and then applies partial braking.
facts.quote:
F -->|Yes, measured deceleration is enough| G["Stand down and keep monitoring"]
    F -->|No| H["Automatic slowing, then partial braking"]

facts.text: Following partial braking, the booklet's decision flow maintains partial braking and re-evaluates if collision is not otherwise unavoidable. If collision is otherwise unavoidable, the system applies maximum safe braking and holds until the operator acts.
facts.quote:
I -->|No| J["Keep partial braking and re-evaluate"]
    I -->|Yes| K["Maximum safe braking, then hold until the operator acts"]

facts.text: For a stationary machine with an object in its projected path, the booklet's decision flow inhibits motion by refusing the move command.
facts.quote: L["Machine stationary with an object in the projected path"] --> M["Motion inhibit: refuse the move command"]

facts.text: The booklet recommends freezing the decision architecture before hardware arrives, using a primary trigger based on predicted swept volume against a stopping-distance envelope: s = v x (t_sense + t_actuate) + v^2 / (2 x a_worst).
facts.quote: freeze the decision architecture before the hardware arrives: a primary trigger based on the predicted swept volume against a stopping-distance envelope, `s = v x (t_sense + t_actuate) + v^2 / (2 x a_worst)`

facts.text: The booklet recommends time to collision as a secondary decision-architecture layer for haul-speed traffic and operator-reaction suppression as a third layer.
facts.quote: with time to collision as a secondary layer for haul-speed traffic and operator-reaction suppression as a third

facts.text: No standard or peer-reviewed study provides tuned time-to-collision or deceleration values for off-road machines; decision-logic values must therefore come from the program's own models and tests.
facts.quote: No standard or peer-reviewed study gives tuned time-to-collision or deceleration values for off-road machines, so the numbers inside the logic must come from the program's own models and tests
